title: Quantum Sensors for Chemistry and Materials Science
authors: Piotr Put, Arjun Pillai, Xuan Hoang Le, Mikhail D. Lukin, Hongkun Park
abstract: The advancement of chemistry and materials science relies on transformative analytical tools which can overcome the sensitivity, spatial resolution, and throughput limitations of conventional techniques. This review explores the application of quantum sensors - specifically optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond - as robust platforms for molecular and materials analysis. We contrast the extreme magnetic sensitivity of macroscopic OPM ensembles with the atomic-scale resolution and multimodal capabilities of solid-state NV centers. We highlight their deployment in zero- to ultralow-field and nanoscale NMR spectroscopy, real-time reaction monitoring, and transient radical and pH detection. Furthermore, we discuss their integration into high-throughput chemical assays and non-destructive materials diagnostics, such as operando battery monitoring. With the ongoing commercialization of these technologies and advances in quantum-enhanced sensitivities, quantum sensors are poised to routinely address complex real-world analytical challenges.
summary: This review surveys the use of advanced quantum sensors, specifically Optically Pumped Magnetometers and NV centers in diamond, to revolutionize chemical and materials analysis. It contrasts OPMs' high bulk sensitivity with NVs' superior nanoscale resolution for applications ranging from battery monitoring to detecting free radicals. The paper argues that these technologies are poised to solve complex real-world analytical challenges.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the inherent limitations of conventional analytical tools—specifically regarding sensitivity, spatial resolution, and throughput—in modern chemistry and materials science.
main_result: Quantum sensors, particularly OPMs and NV centers, are shown to be transformative platforms capable of performing highly sensitive molecular and material diagnostics in real-world settings.
method: The review contrasts two main quantum sensing modalities: Optically Pumped Magnetometers (OPMs) for bulk measurements and Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond for nanoscale, localized probing.
model_or_system: The core physical systems are alkali-metal vapor ensembles used in OPMs and point defects ($	ext{N}$ and vacancy) within the diamond lattice forming NV centers. Sensing relies on monitoring spin states via light absorption/fluorescence (ODMR for NVs).
key_observables: Magnetic field strength, concentration of free radicals ($	ext{ROS}$), $	ext{pH}$, temperature, and spectroscopic signatures (e.g., $	ext{NMR}$ signals) at various spatial scales.
important_parameters: Magnetic sensitivity reaching femtotesla levels; atomic-scale resolution ($\sim 10 	ext{ nm}$) for NVs; operation in zero-to-ultralow magnetic fields ($	ext{ZULF}$).
main_assumptions: The field is maturing toward commercial viability, allowing quantum sensors to routinely address complex analytical challenges previously deemed impossible.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the distinct setups for OPM sensing (using alkali vapors) and NV center sensing (showing energy levels and ODMR measurements), alongside physical examples of their deployment.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a review, first introducing the limitations of current analytical techniques, then detailing the physics and capabilities of OPMs, followed by an in-depth comparison with the multi-modal sensing capabilities of NV centers, concluding with diverse applications like *operando* monitoring.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum physics (spin dynamics, coherence) directly into applied chemistry and materials science diagnostics. The detailed comparison between ensemble averaging (OPMs) and localized defects (NVs) provides a rich case study in translating fundamental quantum measurements to macroscopic engineering problems.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Quantum sensors. (a) Principle of OPM-based sensing. Sample is brought close to glass cell hosting alkali-metal vapor. Atoms in the vapor are optically polarized by a pump laser beam. Sample magnetic field leads to spin evolution, changing the absorption or polarization rotation which is probed with a weak laser beam. (b) Energy-level structure of alkali atoms (here 87Rb) used in OPMs. A laser tuned to (or near) an optical transition in the fine structure of the atom is used as a pump and probe. External magnetic field lifts the degeneracy of the energy levels within the hyperfine manifolds. The population and coherence between these Zeeman sublevels are then optically probed. (c)...

The spectrum reflects J-couplings between nuclear spins in the investigated molecule (2-13C ethanol). Adapted from Ref. (Van Dyke et al., 2022). (b) Chemically specific proton NMR with NVs.
